title: Tail-latency sensitivity: NVLink/PCIe/CUDA driver matrix
content:
Summary:

This note captures an exploratory benchmark suite focused specifically on tail-latency sensitivity across cloud SKUs for A100, H100 and L40S class cards where we varied interconnect topology (NVLink vs PCIe-only), host PCIe generation, and CUDA/driver combinations. The explicit goal was to identify which combinations cause p99 regressions for small-batch, low-concurrency inference workloads (the worst-case behavior that breaks SLAs). This is an investigative, working doc — results are preliminary but actionable.

Why this angle?
- Most prior work looked at sustained throughput or average latency. We saw customer incidents dominated by p95/p99 spikes under specific fleet mixes.
- Hypothesis: host-level topology (NVLink present, PCIe gen, CPU affinity, PCIe root complex sharing) and driver/CUDA scheduler changes disproportionately affect short-lived small-batch requests, KV-cache warmups, and multi-GPU fallbacks.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Models: llama-2-13b (fp16 + int8 quantized runtime), grooming prompt length 64 tokens, response length 128 tokens. Also small decoder-only model toy-2b for microbench.
- Cloud SKUs tested (representative):
  - GCP a2-megatype (A100 80GB, NVLink enabled across-card partitions)
  - AWS p4d-like (A100 multi-gpu with NVLink, PCIe Gen4 host variants)
  - GCP h100-vm (H100 80GB; mixed NVLink/PCIe depending on SKU)
  - Azure L40s (L40s 48GB, PCIe-only in sampled SKUs)
- Driver + CUDA matrix: driver 525/CUDA 11.8, driver 535/CUDA 12.0, driver 550/CUDA 12.2 — we observed a regression candidate in 550 for small-batch scheduling (see Findings).
- Workload sweep: batch sizes {1,2,4}, concurrency {1,4,16}, sequence lengths {32,64,256}, KV-cache warmup vs cached steady state.
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99 latencies (end-to-end), token/sec, GPU utilization (SM%, tensor-core occ), PCIe throughput counters, NVLINK counters where available. Also host CPU load, interrupts per second, and context switch rates.
- Tools: nv-nsight (kernel/driver traces), nvprof/Nsight systems for CUDA timelines, perf + bpftrace for host kernel scheduling, cupy profiler hooks for Python-level breakdown, and a lightweight HTTP harness instrumented with high-resolution timestamps.

Key findings (concise):
1) NVLink presence reduces multi-GPU fallback p99 significantly for model offload patterns. On test matrices where model shard or KV-cache request crossed GPUs, NVLink-enabled SKUs saw median p99 improvement of ~30–45% vs PCIe-only SKUs. This was most pronounced on H100 with driver 535.

2) PCIe host generation impacts cold-start microbursts. PCIe Gen3 vs Gen4 measurements showed ~12% p99 delta for batch=1 cold requests (data transfers for KV cache fills). Notable only for cold requests; steady-state throughput largely unaffected.

3) Driver 550 + CUDA 12.2 exhibited higher scheduler-driven host stalls on H100 for batch=1 concurrent=4 runs. Nsight timelines showed driver-side CPU worker queueing spikes and delayed kernel launches (15–50ms extra in some p99 samples). Rolling back to driver 535 removed those spikes.

4) L40S PCIe-only SKUs had surprisingly stable p50 but p99 volatility due to host-side PCIe interrupts and NUMA-cross memory copies when host CPU affinity was unrestricted. Pinning the inference worker to a single NUMA node and using CUDA pinned memory reduced p99 by ~20%.

5) Small differences in CUDA kernel selection heuristics across driver versions affected quantized int8 kernels: some driver/CUDA combos picked fallback kernels that increased SM utilization but increased latency variance. This was more observable on A100 than H100.

Profiling evidence (examples):
- NVidia Nsight capture (H100 driver 550): saw 20–40ms idle gaps between CPU enqueue and kernel start in p99 traces; correlates with elevated CPU scheduler run-queue lengths.
- PCIe counters: cold fetches moved tens of MB per request (KV cached tensors). On PCIe Gen3 SKUs we saw peaks that saturated the root complex burst budgets causing kernel start backpressure.
- bpftrace snippet highlighted repeated softirq handling on the CPU pinned to the NIC causing jitter; reassigning IRQ affinity to a separate core reduced observed jitter.

Immediate recommendations (practical):
- For small-batch, low-concurrency tiers (our free/low-tier and latency-sensitive routes): prefer NVLink-enabled SKUs where possible. Add an explicit routing policy that prefers NVLink-equipped instances when model sharding or KV-cache sharing is expected.
- Freeze driver family to 535 for H100 fleets until we can reproduce and mitigate the driver 550 scheduler regression. Add driver version to our per-host health telemetry (currently missing detailed driver rollups).
- Default runtime config: allocate pinned host memory for tensor transfers and enforce CPU/core affinity for inference workers (avoid NUMA cross-copy). Provide an automated startup script in our private deploy package to apply these settings.
- For L40S/PCIe-only hosts: enable a micro-batching guardrail (aggregate short bursts for 5–12ms where safe) and increase cold-cache prefetch budget during request admission.

Follow-ups and open questions: 
- Reproduce driver 550 regression across other VM images and bare-metal. Is this specific to cloud hypervisor configuration?
- Dig further into kernel selection differences for int8 kernels across driver/CUDA combos; add microbench for each kernel variant to our optimize recommendations.
- Test with real customer production prompts for a small cohort to validate the p99 improvements when moving to NVLink-enabled SKUs.
- Automate a targeted p99 smoke test that runs on post-image builds (CI gate) to catch driver regressions before fleet rollout.

Appendix: quick run commands and notes (for repeatability)
- Example harness run: ./microbench --model llama-2-13b --quant int8 --batch 1 --concurrency 4 --seq_in 64 --seq_out 128 --warmup 100 --iters 200
- Nsight capture tip: start capture for full 30s around a scheduled microburst; collect both GPU and CPU timeline.
- bpftrace sample to observe softirqs: sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:irq:softirq_entry { @[comm] = count(); }'
- PCIe counter read (example): nvmlDeviceGetPcieTxThroughput / nvmlDeviceGetPcieRxThroughput sampled at 10ms resolution.

Notes on caveats:
- This is an exploratory suite on a limited set of cloud SKUs and image builds; absolute numbers will vary across providers. Focus on directional signals and consistent relative deltas.
- The model choices emphasize decoder-only and quantized paths; if customers use larger context lengths or encoder-decoder models, profile those separately.

If this looks reasonable I propose we:
1) Add a driver-version telemetry field to host heartbeats (owner: SRE, ticket JIRA-ENG-1144).
2) Run an expanded NVLink vs PCIe-only bucket test across a broader set of instance types (owner: serving-runtime, Diego).
3) Draft a short ops playbook for pinning CPU affinity and enabling pinned memory in private deployments (owner: Hannah).

End of note.
